rv.q: In a re-defining performance, Rankin makes Muriel Spark's extraordinary heroine more extraordinary still.
Atmospheric, visceral and cerebral, this is narrative theatre at its very best.

Chloe Lamford’s set, a horseshoe of carpeted steps underneath a giant lampshade inside a large curtain, is also incongruous: it’s an attempt to echo both Miss Brodie’s Italiophile inclinations and the cosseted world of a girls’ school, but it just looks ugly and awkward.

Rankin has all of the charisma needed to bring Brodie to life, so gripping in the play’s first act that the audience gets a taste of what it must have been like to be one of the girls in the “Brodie set”.
It is a well-acted evening of theatre that hits the recognisable beats of Spark's classic.
Thanks to this magnificent production, I now know that it has not.
Harrower, Featherstone and co's mighty rendering breathes vital life into a classic work to reinvent it anew.

Ferocious, visually astonishing, and intellectually rigorous, this co-production with Theatre proves that the shadows of fascism can take root just as easily in the sunlit classrooms of Auld Reekie as they do upon the world stage.

cn.t: Critics praise this revival of Muriel Spark's classic, with Gayle Rankin delivering a sharp, funny, and sexually forthright performance in the title role. Vicky Featherstone's production brings fresh energy to Edinburgh's beloved literary icon.
